Sample Size Comparison

Calculation Details

MeasureValueMethod

What this sample size calculator estimates

This tool estimates the number of completed responses needed to estimate one population proportion, such as the share of customers who choose an option. It uses a normal-approximation confidence interval and assumes a simple random, representative sample. It is not a power analysis for comparing groups or testing a hypothesis.

How to use the inputs

Choose a confidence level, set the maximum margin of error in percentage points, and enter a prior estimate for the proportion. If no estimate is available, 50% is a conservative choice that produces the largest sample size for a fixed confidence level and margin of error. Enter the total population when it is known and sampling without replacement; leave it at 0 for an unknown or very large population.

Formula and finite population correction

Large-population sample: n₀ = z² × p × (1 − p) / E²

Finite population: n = n₀ / [1 + (n₀ − 1) / N]

Here, z is the normal critical value for the selected confidence level, p is the expected proportion as a decimal, E is the margin of error as a decimal, and N is the population size. The calculator rounds the result up because a fraction of a completed response is not possible. For the finite-population estimate, it applies the correction for sampling without replacement. NIST explains the proportion-based sample size inputs and finite-population correction in its Engineering Statistics Handbook.

Worked example

For 95% confidence, a 5-percentage-point margin of error, and an unknown proportion set to 50%, z = 1.96 and p = 0.50. The large-population estimate is 384.16, so plan for at least 385 completed responses. If the population is 1,000 and the sample is drawn without replacement, the finite-population correction reduces the estimate to 278.

Completed responses are not invitations

The result is the number of usable, completed responses. If you expect an 80% response rate, divide the target by 0.80: 385 completed responses would require about 482 invitations. This adjustment is a separate planning step and does not fix nonresponse bias.

Important limitations

This estimate does not account for clustered or stratified sampling, unequal weights, design effects, subgroup reporting, nonresponse bias, or a target for estimating a population mean. Complex surveys and clinical or experimental studies may need different methods and assumptions. CDC's Epi Info population survey guidance also describes its own survey inputs and assumptions. For research decisions, have the study design and sample-size method reviewed by a qualified statistician.

Frequently asked questions

Why is 50% the default expected proportion?

When the true proportion is unknown, 50% maximizes p × (1 − p), giving the most conservative sample size for this proportion-based formula.

What does a 5% margin of error mean?

It means the estimate is planned to be within about 5 percentage points of the population proportion at the selected confidence level, under the stated sampling assumptions.

Does higher confidence require more responses?

Yes. A higher confidence level uses a larger z value, which increases the required sample size when other inputs stay fixed.

Should I enter the total population?

Enter a finite population size when you know the number of eligible people or items and will sample without replacement. Otherwise, use 0 and the calculator will use the large-population estimate.
